title: Redwood POC weekly sync - Lunaris Analytics - cost/econ
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on token throughput versus cost across hosts; reviewed recent benchmark runs, caching gains, and batching tradeoffs. Agreed to run targeted KV-prefix cache test and an additional 10k-token mixed workload to validate tokens/sec/$. Next steps: Redwood to send updated cost model spreadsheet, schedule cache benchmark, customer to provide production prompt mix and traffic distribution.
action_items: Priya Nair | Run KV-prefix cache benchmark (50/50 cached/un-cached) and share logs | 2026-08-25
Alex Chen | Send updated cost model spreadsheet with quantization and batching scenarios | 2026-08-23
Tom Alvarez | Provide production prompt mix and 24h request distribution CSV | 2026-08-24
Maya Patel | Confirm compliance questions for SOC2 scope before pilot transition | 2026-08-28
next_steps: Redwood to run targeted caching benchmark and return tokens/sec and avg latency table
Customer to share prompt set and percent of prefix hits for caching assumptions
Schedule deep-dive demo on dedicated sizing if cache/batching insufficient
Circulate revised cost-per-token model and recommended instance types
transcript: [00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're at the weekly POC sync for Lunaris — cost and econ deep-dive. We have 45 minutes, quick agenda: results recap, caching numbers, batching tradeoffs, and next steps.

[00:18] Maya Patel: Thanks Alex. Appreciate it. I have Jon and Tom on the line, Sara as well — we'll try to keep this focused, we want to get to the numbers and understand the variance we saw last week.

[00:30] Priya Nair: Quick note — apologies if audio glitches, I'm on a flaky hotel wifi. I'll share the slides after. We ran three bench types: baseline host, with prefix KV cache, and batched variant with dynamic batching at 200ms latency target.
[00:50] Jon Rivera: Right, and last week's run had that spike at 95th pctl, we suspected garbage collection on the test VM — was that resolved?

[01:05] Priya Nair: We dug in; that spike correlates with a preemptible eviction on the cloud worker — bad luck. We re-ran an identical workload and numbers stabilized. The rerun is what I'm about to share.
[01:22] Alex Chen: Cool. Can you give us the headline tokens per second per dollar? I know Lunaris cares about tokens/sec/$ more than raw latency for batch workloads.

[01:30] Priya Nair: Headline: baseline (hosted, float32) — median tokens/sec about 820 on an A100-like instance-equivalent; cost model says roughly 0.00032 $/token per 1k tokens — so tokens/sec/$ ~2,560. With 4-bit quant and Redwood's optimized kernels that's up to ~3,900 tokens/sec/$ in our model. With KV-prefix cache and 40% prefix-hit rate we see effective tokens/sec/$ of ~7,100 because cached prefixes avoid autoregressive compute for the first 300 tokens of many requests.
[02:10] Maya Patel: Wait, those cache numbers — 40% hit — are we confident in that given our production prefix distribution? We have some prompts that are very long and unique.

[02:20] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, our logs show about 28% exact-prefix reuse across 30 days, but fuzzy-prefix and semantic similarity could push effective reuse closer to 38-42% if we allow a short canonicalization step.
[02:35] Sara Kim: We also care about tail latency for interactive flows; if caching pushes down cost but increases variability, product is hesitant.

[02:45] Priya Nair: Great point. The caching hits reduce compute and latency for cached prefixes, but cache misses do incur a small lookup overhead. In our runs the 95th pctl improved slightly for cached flows, but cache maintenance can add jitter if eviction storms happen — that's why we recommend TTL tuning and LRU sizing.
[03:10] Jon Rivera: What about batching? Last time we saw batching increase tokens/sec/$ but latency hurt, especially at 95th. What were the config params you used?

[03:20] Priya Nair: For batching we tested three windows: immediate (no batching), 50ms aggregation, and 200ms aggregation. Immediate had lowest median latency but worst tokens/sec/$. 50ms gave a 22% cost improvement, 200ms gave 48% cost improvement but 95th latency rose from ~180ms to ~520ms on our synthetic web UI workload.

[03:45] Alex Chen: So tradeoff is clear. For your background jobs, 200ms batching could be great. For interactive customer-facing endpoints we should aim 50ms or lower. Is that consistent with your SLA targets, Sara?
[03:58] Sara Kim: We want sub-300ms 95th for search suggest flows. 200ms batch pushing us to 520ms is unacceptable there. For nightly scoring jobs, 200ms is fine.

[04:10] Maya Patel: For our revenue-critical product like insights generation, we can accept slightly higher latency if it drops compute by 40% — it's a cost tradeoff we can discuss internally. We need precise cost estimates though, not hand-wavy numbers.
[04:25] Priya Nair: Understood. We'll produce a per-route cost table factoring in typical prompt lengths, prefix percentages, and batching window. That's what Alex will send.

[04:35] Alex Chen: Yup — I'll send the cost spreadsheet with quantization rows, batching sensitivity, and the KV caching effect. We'll include an assumed price-per-hour for both hosted and dedicated scenarios so you can see break-even points.
[04:50] Tom Alvarez: On dedicated sizing — if we go dedicated, do we still get the caching benefits? Also curious about multi-tenancy and isolation, we have compliance concerns.

[05:02] Priya Nair: Yes, caching is part of the runtime and works in Dedicated as well; the difference is you control the GPU pool and we can tune autoscaling. For compliance, Dedicated and Private options include VPC peering and bring-your-own-KMS, which I think you asked about earlier.
[05:18] Maya Patel: We did. SOC2 and KMS are must-haves for pilot-to-prod. Marcus, can you remind on the SOC2 docs ETA?
[05:25] Marcus Lee: We're updating the SOC2 report for 2026 Q2; I can share the control matrix and effort to scope LUN into the attestation — will send by EOD Thursday.

[05:35] Jon Rivera: Thanks. Back to numbers: can you walk through a concrete example — say, a 1k-token prompt with 30% prefix hits, median latency target 200ms, what instance type and cost do you recommend?

[05:50] Priya Nair: Example: For hosted, with G4dn-like instance-equivalent and 4-bit quant, median is roughly 250ms per 1k token turn and cost per 1k tokens about $0.012 in our baseline. With 30% cache hits effective cost falls to ~$0.0077 per 1k tokens. Dedicated (reserved) using an H100-like pool with mixed precision and batch optimizations reduces that to ~$0.005 per 1k tokens at scale, assuming 50% utilization.

[06:25] Tom Alvarez: That utilization assumption is key — our traffic is spiky; nights are low, midday bursts. If utilization drops to 20%, dedicated per-token cost increases, so we need burst capacity options.

[06:40] Alex Chen: Redwood Dedicated supports burst capacity and configurable autoscaling policies — you can reserve base and allow bursts to hosted capacity with policy-based routing which keeps costs predictable and avoids wasted committed spend.
[06:55] Maya Patel: I like the idea of hybrid — reserve for baseline, burst for peaks. How do we measure the break-even point to decide reserve size?

[07:05] Priya Nair: We'll include a break-even calculator in the spreadsheet: inputs are avg qps, p95 latency requirement, percent cached, and percent reserved. It outputs projected monthly cost for hosted vs dedicated and delta.
[07:18] Sara Kim: Can you also show sensitivity to quantization quality? We saw small regressions with 4-bit on a few prompts last week.

[07:25] Priya Nair: We'll add a QC column: inference quality delta (BLEU/ROUGE-like proxy) for 4-bit vs float32 on your prompt set; if regressions exceed your threshold we recommend 8-bit per-layer or mixed precision selectively on output-critical layers.
[07:40] Alex Chen: Tom, you'll provide the prompt mix and traffic distribution so Priya can tune the cached-hit model assumptions — that's an action item. Anything else on the benchmark methodology?

[07:50] Tom Alvarez: Can you include a run that simulates our blended workload: 60% short queries (<=150 tokens), 30% medium (150-800), 10% long (>800)? We have different caching behavior across those bins.
[08:05] Priya Nair: Yes — we'll run mixed workload with those proportions. Also we'll output per-bin tokens/sec/$ and tail latency. Expect results within 48 hours.
[08:18] Maya Patel: On security — one more ask: can you show how audit logs look in Private deploy versus Hosted for compliance reviewers? They need event-level access and KMS key rotation proof.
[08:30] Marcus Lee: I'll attach sample audit log schema and the KMS rotation policy doc. We'll also annotate where logs are stored and retention options.
[08:42] Jon Rivera: Regarding the cache, what eviction policy and size do you recommend for our median request size? We want to avoid thrashing.

[08:50] Priya Nair: For your workload size distribution we'd likely recommend an LRU with TTL of 24 hours and a size cap tuned to hold ~10k unique prefixes — we'll recommend exact numbers after we see Tom's prompt-cardinality data.
[09:05] Sara Kim: Also question: If we canonicalize slightly (strip user ids from prompts) — how risky is that for downstream correctness?
[09:12] Tom Alvarez: We have a small internal mapping layer that normalizes some tokens; I'd be comfortable providing that so long as product signs off.

[09:20] Alex Chen: Good. Let's capture the immediate deliverables — Redwood runs KV-prefix cache benchmark; Redwood shares cost spreadsheet and dedicated break-even calc; Lunaris shares prompt mix and production traffic CSV; Marcus shares SOC2 artifacts and audit log schema.
[09:35] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Timeline okay: we need numbers by early next week to decide reserved capacity for September pilot.
[09:45] Alex Chen: We'll target sending the spreadsheet by Monday 8/23, caching benchmark by Tuesday 8/25. Is that feasible, Priya?

[09:52] Priya Nair: Yes, feasible. One note — for the cache benchmark we need a small stub of your canonicalizer if you want semantic prefix hits included. Tom, can you provide a quick script or rules?
[10:03] Tom Alvarez: I'll drop a 2-file sample and rules in the shared drive by tomorrow.
[10:10] Jon Rivera: Minor tangent — any thoughts on model fallbacks? If H100 capacity is constrained can we route to a cheaper variant automatically?

[10:18] Priya Nair: Yes, smart routing supports fallback to compatible model variants; the key is to quantify quality delta so we can auto-fallback with an SLA flag — we'll add that to the spreadsheet as a tolerance column.
[10:28] Sara Kim: Great. One last product question: will streaming affect batching economics? We use streaming for some flows.

[10:34] Priya Nair: Streaming tends to reduce batchability since you often want low-latency first token. For streaming-first flows batching gains are smaller; however KV caching still helps because it truncates generation time. We'll measure streaming and non-streaming separately.
[10:50] Alex Chen: Ok folks — wrapping up. Recap of action items in the chat and I'll follow up with the Google Sheet link. Any final Qs?
[10:58] Maya Patel: None from me. Thanks team.
[11:02] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll reconvene same time next week unless otherwise needed. Bye.
[11:05] (call end)
